44TH ANNUAL REPORT. 


In reviewing another year we desire to acknowledge God’s blessing 
in the privileges granted to the Association of serving the Young 
Men of the City of Montreal. 

This Association has always maintained the closest alliance with 
the affiliated Associations in their world-wide work. During the past 
year it was represented at the following Conventions :— 

The World’s Jubilee Convention, London, Eng., June 6-10, 1894. 

The Provincial Convention, Belleville, January 21-24, 1895. 

The 31st International Convention at Springfield, May, 1895. 

The 25th Annual Conference of General Secretaries at Hartford, 
Conn., May, 1895. 

We have continued our contributions to the Provincial work, also 
to the International Committee and its Foreign work for the Young 
Men of the Orient, as well as co-operated with the Springfield 
Training School in its development of men for future service. But 
in the matter of extension we have not even begun to do our duty. 
Every active member should have some part, no matter how small, 
in extending this beneficent work to these millions of young men of 
less favored lands. Read carefully the Extension Committee’s report, 
and see that your name is in the list for 1895-96. 


GIFTS. 


With gratitude to God we acknowledge three special gifts received 
during the year, We look upon them as the forerunners of other 
gifts and bequests which are to follow. 

First.—The valuable Medical Library and furnishings which 
belonged to the late Dr. George Fenwick, and which was given to 
the Association by Mrs. Fenwick at the request of her late husband.’ | 

SEcOND.—The gift of the rear half of the lot between the Associ- 
ation Building and Knox Church, size 69.10 x 64.9 feet, at a cost of 


9 


$10,000. This valuable donation was made by Mr.Warden King, our 
esteemed Director and Treasurer, who has the thanks of the Associa- 
tion for this thoughtful and generous act. As a matter of history, 
the lot upon which this Building stands with the Annex now donated, 
was the original plan of lot which the Directors tried to secure 
before beginning the present Building. They did not succeed at 
that time. Now it has come as a glad surprise. 

We give the “‘ outline plans ” of the proposed Educational Annex. 
As soon as it becomes a ‘“‘ fact” the Association will be able to offer 
instruction in Manual and Industrial lines as follows :— 

Forging, Plumbing, Carpentry, Pattern-Making; Elementary, 
Freehand, Mechanical and Architectural Drawing; Chemistry, and 
Electricity’ Besides these there will be additional accommodation 
for an increase in the Commercial and English courses. The 
Directors have decided that this Annex is to be erected without add- 
ing to the present fixed charges on the property. May God put the 
thought and action into the heart of some of His servants, who will 
see this splendid opportunity for an investment which will enable the 
Association to reach and influence from 700 to 1000 young men each 
year who are wage-earners and who long for these advantages in the 
line of self-improvement. Fully one-half of this number would be 
from the mechanical and industrial classes. The cost will be from 
$30,000 to $40,000, including equipments. 

Turrp.—The valuable ‘‘collection” of specimens in Natural 
History and Geology which has been made by the Cote St. Antoine 
Agassiz Society has been donated to the Association by Mr. Thomas 
Patton and the members of the Agassiz Society who had_ the 
“collection” in charge. This donation is made in the memory of 
the late Willie Shaw, who was the founder of the Society. These 
friends have the thanks of the Association. The Directors requested 
the Chautauqua Class to form an Agassiz Society among the members, 
so that the work may continue on the same lines. 


THE BUILDING. 


The Directors have to report a larger use of the privileges offered 
in the Building than the previous year. Its doors are open fourteen 
hours of every day, and, while the privileges are largely for the

members’ use, still every young man is welcomed, and he can receive 
counsel and advice on the line of his personal need. We are pleased 
to report the rapid growth of this line of work, and the Association 
wishes it to be understood that, in addition to its direct work with 
young men, it is always ready to co-operate with friends and relatives 
on behalf of young men in whom they are interested, wherever they 
may reside. The following will illustrate:—One gentleman wrote 
from a Western city, soliciting our help in behalf of a relative who 
was here in great trouble. We were able to secure his return at 
once, and the result has been an entire change in the young man’s 
life. A gentleman solicited our interest on his brother’s behalf, who 
was in great distress and trouble in another city. Through the 
co-operation of the Secretary of that Association we were able to 
secure his immediate return. His brother was most grateful, and he 
has since joined the Association. A lady in a distant city solicited 
our interest in a young man whose life was being uselessly frittered 
away here. We secured him as a member, and his life has been 
completely changed. His testimony is: ‘‘ Of all the money I spend, 
the membership fee in the Association does the most for me.” 


FINANCE. 


It is with special gratification that we refer you to the financial 
statement for the year. Notwithstanding the severe business depres- 
sion the full amount needed has been raised, and all the bills have 
been paid, thus enabling the Association to continue the unbroken 
record for the past six years. For this happy result the Association 
is indebted to the untiring efforts of the Finance Committee, who 
have labored most earnestly throughout the whole year. The mem- 
bers ought to realize that no other Committee in the Association 
gives one-half the time and effort to the development of this work 
as is so freely given by the members of this Committee. 

We call special attention to this item in the statement: $1140.03 
is the amount paid by the Current Expense Account to balance the 


‘‘ Property Account.” This is true, notwithstanding the fact that the 


Building is fully ‘‘ leased.” ‘This means that the present mortgage 
debt on the Building must be reduced by $26,000 in order that the 
property may pay its legitimate charges and give the Association the 


13 


use of its rooms free of rental. We trust this may be speedily 
accomplished. 
MEMBERSHIP. 

The membership shows an increase of $1,144 over last year in the 
amount received from fees. With the exception of January, there 
was an increase in receipts every month. This good showing is 
wholly due to the untiring efforts of Mr. W. F. Chapman, Office 
Secretary. This year we hope to plan a ‘‘membership campaign,” 
so as to thoroughly canvass all young men of the city. This has 


never been done. 
PHYSICAL. 


From the Physical report you will see that the Gymnasium has 
continued its good work, and is still one of our most attractive 
features. 388 Senior and 115 Junior members received physical 
examination. Many young men who come for the Gymnasium become 
interested in other Departments of the work, and some have been led 
thereby into the religious meetings and out into the Christian life. 


EVENING CLASSES. 


The Evening Classes as a power to attract young men are even 
now a rival to the Gymnasium, and will soon equal it. The report 
shows 552 entries in the various classes were made in October, 
being an increase of 217 over last year. Instruction was given in 
nine branches. Without exception those who persevered in the 
work acknowledged the great benefits received. At the Educational 
Exhibit of the International Convention at Springfield, the work 
done by the Phonography Class received honorable mention. We 
know of three, and doubtless there are many others, who were 
attracted to the Association through the Educational Classes, and 
then came to the religious meetings, where they were led to take 
Jesus Christ as their Lord and Saviour, and are now active workers. 


RELIGIOUS. 


Our religious meetings have been maintained during the year. 
234 gospel meetings and Bible classes have been held, with a total 
attendance of 10,604 young men. We are glad to report an increase 
over last year in the average attendance of all but one meeting. The 


14 


Young Men’s Bible Class increased from an average of 71 to 96, the 
largest attendance it has ever reached; the Men’s Meeting on 
Sunday afternoon held an average attendance of 170; the Young 
Men’s Meeting on Saturday evening, an average of 79; and the Sun- 
day morning Bible Class, an average of 15. A ten-days’ Mission to 
young men was conducted by Messrs. Elliott and Butts. While the 
attendance was not large, there have been many permanent results in 
the conversion of young men who are now on our active working 
force. . 

While reporting the above facts about the religious work, we are 
painfully conscious that neither the employés nor the active workers 
have recognized the unequalled opportunities which this building 
and its many departments, now thronged with young men, affords for 
practical Christian effort. That young men can be _ specially 
influenced by their fellow young men in making a decision for the 
Christian life, is no longer a question. In this the record of results 
is not what it ought to be or what it might have been—and the past 
year’s opportunity is gone. We are convicted of failure in this 
important trust. May a truer consecration and a better organization 
of the whole work with this point in view lead to larger results in the 

uniting of more young men to Jesus Christ. 


JUNIOR. 


The Junior Department. has maintained its efficiency. Their 
membership shows an increase of 38. Their Executive Committee 
has done effective work, and the number who graduate into the 
Senior Department each year proves what a strength this is to the 
general work. A better organized personal work force would secure 
larger spiritual results here as in the Senior Department. Let that 
be the aim of the new committee. This Department requires some 
new furnishings and equipment, which must be secured for the Fall 
work. 

We have not seen any new men from our force go into Christian 
work during the year. Two of our members, however, are now at 
McGill College, having Christian work in view at the completion of 
their course. Mr. C. B, Powter purposes taking a second year at 
the Springfield Training School, and is considered by the Instructors 


r 

” 
a 
my, 


15 


one of their best men. Mr. Percy H. Cushing, who has been an 
efficient Assistant for the past two years, will enter the Springfield 
School in September for further training. It is a pleasant fact to 
record that the men from Montreal have done our Association honor 
both while at Springfield and after they have entered active work. 

We are glad to announce that the Directors have secured the 
services of Mr. C. K. Calhoun, of Lindsay, Ont., who has had two 
years in Association work, and who will take the position of 
Assistant Secretary in September. He is considered an able man, 
having exceptional qualities for this special work. We ask our 
members to give him a cordial welcome. 


OUR NEEDS. 
In.view of the past, what are our needs ? 


1.—To make the Bible study department the most prominent 
feature of the work. Plan for a series of Bible Class courses in 
special lines by competent leaders. 

2.—Make a larger “appropriation” for the spiritual work of the 
Association. Organize and develop a larger force of personal 
workers amongst the Active Members. This work can never be 
overtaken from the office end. 

3.—Do not concentrate all the religious work in the Building ; 
spread out. Plan for reaching men in other sections of the city by 
deputation meetings. 

4.—Plan the Evening Class Work .so that each branch of study 
will include a two years’ course. Aim for this continued work. Let 
the teacher give each member an examination before entering. 

s.—Plan for a number of courses of practical educational talks in 
Current Topics, economics, and other lines. These will interest 
and educate a large number not attached to the Educational 
Classes. 

6.—Advertise the whole Association work more liberally. Aim. 
for the great industrial class of young men. 

7.—Pian for the Social Work on a broader scale. Develop an 
intermingling of interests and Departments. Foster a deeper 
enthusiasm in the Association on the part of the members. Aim to 


a 


16 


get each member out of the ‘‘ value received” idea into the spirit of 
the broad movement. 

8.—Work for one thousand new volumes to be added to the 
Library. 

g.—Plan for a larger financial constituency of citizens. Hun- 
dreds have never been informed about the work or asked to contribute. 
Endeavor to secure an increased amount from present subscribers. 
Many are giving the same amount which they did when the work 
was only one-fourth as large as at present. 

10.—Let the Gymnasium Class work be developed. Guard against 
the tendency to use the Gymnasium for recreation and amusement 
only. 

Let these vital questions be thoroughly discussed by the Committees 
in charge at the opening of the year, and the result must mean an 
advance movement on the whole line of work. Aim for thoroughness 
in every department. 

Above all, we call upon every active member to make this special 
work a subject of his daily prayer. Without this divine wisdom and 
co-operation their efforts will be unavailing in securing the salvation 
of young men.

J. Murray Smith joined the Association in 1879, and during twelve 
years ably filled the position of Director, which he held at the time 
of his death. He was President in 1883 and 1884. His practical 
interest in the development of this work was of the greatest possible 
value to the young men of the city.

FINANCE. 


Herewith are the Financial Statements of the Association for the year ending 30th 
April, 1895, duly audited by Messrs. P. S. Ross & Sons. 

The Association again ends its fiscal year with a small balance on the credit side 
($42.84), all outstanding accounts having been liquidated. We have reason to be 
thankful to our Heavenly Father for this result, in a year of such financial s¢vess as 
the past has been. 

The largely increased revenue from memberships is a most pleasing evidence of the 
expanding circle of the Association usefulness. This augmentation is due not only to 
the efforts of the Membership Committee but to the Association mzemders themselves, 
both Senior and Junior, in making the advantages and benevolences more thoroughly 
known. 

The Finance Committee, having to face a prospective shortage of about $1,500, 
set to work early in the year on their arduous task, and it is most gratifying to them 
that the generous kindness of so many friends who have contributed has enabled 
them to bring it to a successful conclusion and to close the year without debt. 

To all the friends who have thus helped they extend their hearty thanks. 


WARDEN KING, DOW: ROSS, 


Treasurer. Chairnuian.

The following list includes no membership fees except those paid by Sustaining 
Members, who are indicated by an asterisk (*). A large number of Full and Limited 
Members pay their fee simply as a recognition of their interest in the work, but it is 
impossible to indicate them without publishing the membership roll, for which we 
have not space. They will please accept our most hearty thanks.

This does not include any who joined during April, nora large number whose 
membership recently expired, and who will undoubtedly renew within a few weeks. 
If these were included, the total would be at least 1co greater. No special effort has 
been made to increase the membership, but the number of applications received each 
month, especially in September and October, was very encouraging. During the 
coming year we hope to bring the membership up to 2,000. 


W. GODBEE BROWN, 
Chairman. 


EVENING CLASSES AND LECTURES. 


The following statement concerning the work of the past year is submitted :—

In addition to the regular Evening Class work, three Special Courses have been 
carried out. 

The first Course of Ten Lectures on “‘ Canadian Political History,” given by Mr. 
Herbert B. Ames, as follows :— 


LecturE I. The Old French Régime in Canada. 
ne II. The British Constitution. 
‘¢ III. The Constitution and Government of the United States. 
‘¢ IV. How the Canadian Constitution was Developed. 
ibs V. The Canadian Constitution. The B.N.A. Acts. Part I. 
‘¢ VI. The Canadian Constitution. The B.N.A. Acts.: Part If. 
‘¢ VIL. The Dominion Parliament in Motion. 
‘* VIII. Canada’s Political Parties. 
‘¢ IX. Canada’s Future Destiny. 
im X. The Right of Dominion Suffrage. 


30 


The popularity and utility of this Course warranted the Committee in publishing 
2,000 pamphlets containing the Full Outline as prepared by Mr. Ames. 

A Second Course a3 Six Medical Lectures was given by Dr. W. S. Morrow as 
follows :— 

LECTURE I. The Rights and Wrongs of the Stomach. 

‘¢ II. Breathing and Consumption. 

aF ATL Circulation. 

«¢ IV. Work and Over-Work. 

ih V. The Organs of the Mind. 

‘¢ VI. Heredity, ‘‘ To the third and fourth generation.” 

These lectures held a large attendance of the young men who had been taking class 
work in the Physical Department, and must have produced good results. 

A Course of Three Lectures were given by Mr. McIntosh to the members interested 
in Amateur Photography. The attendance at these was not as large as we had 
expected. 

To each of these Lecturers who freely made so valuable a contribution to our 
Educational work we hereby tender the thanks of the Association. 


E. I. REXFORD, 
Chairman.

G. F. Hartt, $25; Sir Donald Smith, $25 ; a lady, ie and and also money sub- 
scribed by the members, about $35.

The following New Books were added :—Social Evolution, by Benj. Kidd; The 
Meeting-Place of Geology and History, by Sir Wm. Dawson ; Across the Atlantic, 
by R. A. Naylor: Poems, Songs and Sonnets, by Robert Reid ; Modern Skepticism, 
by Mark Hopkins ; Jamaica at the Columbian Exhibition, by C. J. Ward ; Modern 
Ideas of Evolution, by Sir Wm. Dawson; History for Ready Reference, 2 vols. ; 


OL 


Rajah of Dah, by Geo. Manville Fenn; The New Acts of rhe Apostles, by. A. T. 
Pierson ; The New Era, by Rev. Josiah Strong ; Ascent of Man, by Drummond ; 
Daniel Webster’s Works ; Photographic Bulletin, by Anthony ; In the Heart of the 
Rockies, Wulf the Saxon, and When London Burned, by G. A. Henty ; Renaissance 
and Modern Art, by Wm. Goodyear ; Walks and Talks in the Geological Field, by 
Alex’r Winchell ; From Chaucer to Tennyson, by H. A. Beers; Europe in the rgth 
Century, by H. P. Judson; the Growth of the English Nation, by Kath. Coman and 
Elizabeth Kendall ; Simon Jasper, by Mark Guy Pearse ; The Student’s History of 
England, by Gardiner ; Beside the Bonnie Briar Bush, by Ian Maclaren. 

In the Reading Room we have Io dailies, 1 tri-weekly, 2 semi-weeklies, 54 weeklies 
and 56 monthlies. 

New covers have been purchased for the magazines, and new files for the papers 
have been obtained. 

J. MCDONALD OXLEY, 


Chairman. 


YOUNG MEN’S MEETING. 


The attendance at the meetings has been about the same as that of last year, the 
total being 3,952, or an average attendance of 76, as against 77 last year. We are 
sorry to have to report a decrease, however small, but trust the work done has been 
equally as effective and lasting as in years gone by. Though we cannot show in 
figures the amount of work done, or the good resulting from it, we have every reason 
to believe that much good has been done and that our Heavenly Father has honored 
and blessed the work of this Committee in their efforts to advance His kingdom 
among men. Many have manifested an interest in their soul’s salvation, and we 
believe many have sought and found Christ as their Saviour, while others have been 
strengthened and encouraged in their Christian work. 

We can see where we have been blessed with success and where we have failed, 
and trust the failures may prove a means of encouragement to a higher and more 
faithful life on the part of each member of the Committee, and for the success we 
give all the praise to Him whose we are and whom we serve, thanking Him for the 
great privilege He has granted us of being workers together with Christ for the 
salvation of men. Respectfully submitted, 

JAS. R. GREIG, 
Secretary. 


MEN’S MEETING. 


During the past season 40 meetings have been held, with an average attendance of 
170; total attendance of 6,132 young men. | 

Your Committee desires to express its thanks to the ministers of this city, and also 
to Sir Wm. Dawson, Dr. S. P. Robins, and Geo. Hague, Esq., who have occupied 
our platform, and we have the satisfaction of knowing that the words which they 
have spoken have been the means of the conviction and conversion of some of their 


o2 


hearers. Your Committee is also indebted to a number of the City Choirs for their 
assistance at different times. 

The presence of the members of the Asssociation who may not be engaged in 
Sabbath-school or other Christian work at the hour of our meeting would not only 
help the Committee, but, we have reason to think, would be an example to many 
others, who might be brought under the influcnce of the Divine Spirit, and thus led 
to become useful members of our Association and churches. 

J. HAMILTON FERNS, 
Chairman. 


SUNDAY AFTERNOON BIBLE-CLASS. 


This class has held an aggregate attendance of 4,968, being an increase of 1,373 
over the preceding year; the weekly average being 96, the highest ever attained. 
This large increase is partly due to the class being merged into the Elliott and Butts 
meetings two Sundays in December, but outside of these meetings a very large 
increase is shown. We are indebted to Sir Wm. Dawson, who conducted the class 
fora month during the summer ; also to Messrs. J. Ritchie Bell, D. W. Ross and 
W. F. Chapman, who have taken charge during the absence of Mr. Budge. 

The study during the past year has been most interesting, being of the Exodus and 
the Journeying of the Children of Israel to the Promised Land, followed by character 
studies of the principal characters in the books of Judges, Ist and 2nd Samuel, etc. 

Another feature has recently been added :—On the last Sunday in each month we 
take up a topical study on such subjects as ‘‘ Faith,” * Prayer,” etc., which takes the 
form of an open Bible study, the object being to help members in plans and methods 
of personal study. 

Through our monthly collection we have been enabled to pay the printing and other 
expenses connected with the class ; to send flowers to sick members in the hospitals ;. 
to relieve several cases of distress ; and to send a delegate from the class, Mr. G. P. 
Tasker, to the annual Inter-Provincial Convention held at Belleville in January last. 
On the last Sunday in December we held our annual Bible-Class Tea. The testi- 
monies given by each member of the value of the class to him personally were very 
encouraging, and show the influence it has on the lives of so many young men. 

We wish to thank Messrs. Lomax, Walmsley, and the class quartette, who have 
kindly assisted in the music. Respectfully submitted, 

LEWIS A. WINTER, 
Chairman. 


SUNDAY MORNING BIBLE-CLASS. 


A record of the attendance has only been kept since September Ist. During that 
time there have been 35 sessions, with an average attendance of 16. Two courses of 
lessons have been foliowed,—the first a series of topical studies in the book of 
Proverbs, and the second a series of the most familiar Psalms. Both of these courses. 
have been deeply tnteresting and helpful to those who attended. 

W. F. CHAPMAN, 
Leader. 


39 


INVITATION. 


Your Committee has met each Saturday night during the year for the purpose of 
handing out invitations on the street corners, with an average attendance of five 
workers. Seven of the members have gone to other cities, and were obliged, there- 
fore, to tender their resignation. ‘The work has been enconraging and helpful to 
each one of us. On many occasions we have not only been able to give out an invi- 
tation to our meeting, but also to give information concerning the Association and its 
work. Some 30,000 invitations have been handed out during the year. While this 
work is the means of bringing many young men to the Saturday night meeting, we 
do not think it should be depended upon for reaching all the young men that should 
be invited to this meeting. A card received at the street corner will often bring a 
young man to the meeting, but it has not the weight of a personal invitation from an 
active member. ‘There are many young men in the Association who would like to be 
of service in the cause of Christ, but who seem to overlook the fact that the Saturday 
night meeting offers them one of the grandest opportunities. This is ¢2e work of the 
Association, and it is a privilege for the members to have such a meeting to invite 
young men to. 

We would like to see, and would suggest, that every active member of the 
Association become a member of this Committee, azd work. 

Let every active member realize the responsibility of attending Saturday evening 


meeting himself and introducing young men. 
GEO. COMRIE, 


Chairman. 


PHYSICAL DEPARTMENT. 


Each succeeding year has shown greater results in this department. Greater interest 
and enthusiasm has been manifested, and new features have been added. 


OUT-DOOR. 


The Association has leased land from the Government and the fishing rights of a 
lake near St. Agathe, and purpose using it as a summer camp for our members. It is 
a charming spot, and affords opportunity for a delightful holiday at trifling expense. 
Last year 53 members took advantage of this privilege. 

The Bicycle Club organized at the close of last year has proved a popular feature. 
Weekly runs have been held, with a good attendance. The present season opened 
with a largely increased membership. The new officers gave the members and their 
friends a reception, which was very successful. 

The Committee made the same arrangements for the Shamrock Grounds as for the 
previous year. The interest in Lacrosse was maintained, and the practices well 
attended. Several strong players have been developed, and the Association has a 
good team. It has been found almost impossible, however, to arrange games with 
other teams, owing to the lack of grounds. The same may be said of Rugby football. 

The fact of not having the use of suitable athletic grounds makes us realize more 
than ever before the great opportunity the Association is missing to reach and 
influence the lives of young men. 


34 


The Snowshoe Club secured the use of the large hall at the Athletic Club House 
for the season, and, although the sport appears to be on the decline, the Association 
trampers had a good season. The veterans’ night, when over 100 put in an appear- 
ance, was a new departure. The Athletic Events and the At Home were both up to 
the usual standard. 

The interest in Basket Ball has continued to increase. More members have been 
playing on teams than any previous year, there being a total of 161. Three different 
schedules were maintained : one among the Business Men, with four teams competing, 
which was won by the team captained by Mr. C. C. Holland ; another among the 
Boys, with five teams (for the third consecutive time the Stars proved the victors of 
the Boys’ series) ; and a third among the Young Men, with six teams, which, after a 
close and exciting series of contests, was won by the Granites, who thus become the 
champions of 1895. 

The interest shown this winter in Bowling has been remarkable. The alleys were 
crowded. Individual competitions were held for weekly, monthly and annual prizes. 
A Tournament, in which six teams competed, was successfully carried out. The 
Granites proved victors, with an average score of 1,201. 


INDOOR. 


During the past year almost 1,100 men and boys have been using the privileges 
offered through our Gymnasium and Baths. 503 new members have been examined 
(388 young men and 115 boys), making a total since opening of 2,274. 

Almost every available locker is in use. 

The average weekly class attendance has been 435. Each class meets twice a 
week, and the class averages are as follows :—Advanced, II ; Intermediate, 21 ; 
Elementary, 40 ; Junior, 31 ; Boys, 49; Business Men, 17, Students, 13 ; Pastors, 6, 
The attendance during the second week of November was 725, the highest on 
record. 

A series of four Confidential Talks by the Physical Director were given during 
April, in the Young Men’s Meeting Room, with good attendance and beneficial 
results... 

A new feature in our work was the Gymnastic Exhibition held in the Windsor 
Hall on 20th November last, under the distinguished patronage of His Excellency 
the Governor-General. From every point of view the Exhibition was a decided 
success. We are greatly indebted to the Montreal Orchestral Association for their 
kind assistance. 

The work done in this Department under the wise and efficient direction of Mr. 
Wm. H. Ball, the Physical Director, cannect be too highly spoken of. He has been 
ably seconded in his work by Mr. H. H. Field, Assistant Director, and a corps of 29 
Volunteer Leaders. 

We appreciate very much the faithful services of our Medical Examiners, W. H. 
Drummond, M.D.; ‘W. Grant Stewart? M.D.; R.C. Kirkpatrick, M.D.; D. J. 
Evans, M.D. ; and desire to extend to them our sincere thanks. 


WILLIAM TEES, 
Chatrman.

SOCIAL AND RECEPTION DEPARTMENT. 


During the past year, through the kindness of the choirs and ladies of Dominion 
Square Methodist, St. Paul’s Presbyterian, and Olivet Baptist Church, music and 
refreshments were provided for the monthly socials. We were glad to notice an 
increase in the attendance at those social gatherings. While a few of our older 
members attend, the greater majority are the younger and newer men. It should be 
the endeavor of our older members to be present at these socials. They would 
encourage and help by their presence and become acquainted with our younger 
members. It is impossible for any Committee to make our building as attractive 
socially as it should be unless our members are willing to set aside these evenings for 
the good of the work. The Committee plan and arrange for the gatherings ; it lies 
with our members to bring the Committee’s work toa successful issue. We realize 
the weak point in the social work, and would impress the responsibility of it upon 
each member. ; 

In December the Committee engaged Miss Jessie Alexander, of Toronto, to give 
an evening of elocution, combined with a good musical programme by local talent. 

A new feature was introduced in the form of a closing social to the members of the 
educational department. Each class added something to the programme. The walls 
were hung with fine exhibitions of freehand and mechanical drawings executed by the 
drawing classes. Two speeches and a song were given in French, blackboard 
examples by the arithmetic and shorthand classes, several two-minute talks by 
members of the Chatauqua Class, and testimonies from a number of members of the 
different classes showing their appreciation of the benefits of this department of the 
Association. The musical part of the program and refreshments were provided by 
the ladies of Olivet Church. 

The Hallowe’en gathering and New Year’s Day Reception and Concert was held 
with an unusually good attendance, and especially the latter, which was one of the 
best ever held. The rooms were tastefully decorated, and the addition of an 
orchestra lent a new charm to the building. 

Three Sunday evening teas have been held for strangers, who enjoyed and appre- 
ciated the kindness of the Association in this direction. 

The evening reception department has been handicapped by being unable to 
secure enough members willing to devote the time necessary to this important work. 
Those who have taken this work in hand have been faithful in the discharge of their 
duties, and deserve the highest commendation. Here is required faithful, untiring 
energy, combined with a knowledge of the work, that in welcoming strangers and 
shewing them the building, the various departments may be carefully explained. 
They have also arranged and carried out a chess tournament, which created a great 
deal of interest, and have endeavored in various ways to make the building attractive 
during the evenings. 

The Committee desire to thank those who have helped them during the year. 
More perhaps than any other Committee we look for assistance to the friends of the 
Association, especially the ladies, and their co-operation is as gratefully received and 
acknowledged as it is heartily and generously given. We would not forget our own 
members who so kindly assisted at the Hallowe’en gathering and in the decorations 
for the New Year’s Reception. 

Respectfully submitted, JOHN W. ROSS, 
Chatrman. 


36 


EXTENSION FUND. 


While we are pleased to report an increase in the amount of money passing through 
our hands in this branch of the work, we regret that a greater interest is not taken 
generally by the members. 

As a whole, the Association has fallen off somewhat in its donations through the 
envelope, and the gross increase is due to a special donation of $250. 

The International Committee could accomplish much greater results if more money 
were placed in their hands. Men are ready and anxious to go, ‘‘The fields are white 
unto the harvest,” but for lack of means they have to turn a deaf ear to the cry from 
foreign lands. 

Just think of at least twelve million young men to every Association Secretary 
who devotes his whole time to the work in the dark places of the earth. 

Since our last report two have gone to India, Mr. A. P. Stockwell to Calcutta, and 
Mr. Davis to Madras; Mr. Heib goes immediately to Ceylon and Mr. Lion to 
China. 

Ways AND MEANS.—There are about 35 regular contributors, and the amounts 
vary from $250 downward.

37 


JUNIOR DEPARTMENT. 


We cannot present the report of this department of the work without speaking of 
the great responsibility that we feel is resting upon us as we seek to carry it on, and 
the great privilege God has given each one of us in being co-workers with Him 
among the bright lives whom we have been seeking, during this year, to lead toa 
knowledge of Jesus Christ as a personal friend and Saviour. 

The Executive Committee has worked faithfully during the year, and great harmony 
has prevailed in every branch of the work. This result has been attained by the 
spiritual part being made prominent at every one of its meetings. The members 
have gathered together regularly for prayer for a blessing upon each branch of the 
work, and from fifteen to twenty minutes have been spent in this way before or after 
each regular monthly meeting, and we are therefore not surprised that God has been 
with us. 

The working force has been as follows, viz :— 


CSERELEE She th ee IN nr 6 
ROMINA Cee Diem a eco arte aly Cavelene 73 
With an Executive Committee of.......... IO 


Our efforts have been to develop among our members a deeper interest in prayer 
and Bible study, and to this end we have used the Scripture Union, by which all boys 
have read a portion of God’s word every day, to which we have added a special 
course of Bible study for the older workers. In the line of prayer, a neat ‘‘ prayer 
slip” was issued, allotting different parts of the work to the days of the week, and 
these have been distributed among the Christian boys, who have been asked to pray 
for these definitely. This has been used of God in bringing a great and lasting 
blessing to many young lives and to the Association generally. 

Our religious meetings have been good, and the attendance slightly in advance of 
last year, viz. an average of 63. We know that many have been led to the Lord 
Jesus Christ and our Christian workers have been developed, and we feel that there 
are boys growing up in our midst who will become useful and fruitful workers in the 
Senior Department. 

Six regular training classes have been held, and have proved of great benefit. 
These classes have been and still are the greatest power in our whole work, and results 
are sure to follow ; but, on account of the nature of our members, it is very hard to 
see any very definite development yet ; but we know the seed is there, and God will 
make it grow and bear fruit in His good time. 

Our regular monthly visit to the General Hospital has been held, and we now have 
access to all the wards, where hymns are sung and papers are distributed, giving joy 
and gladness to many of the inmates, and bringing a reflex blessing upon those who 
perform this service. 

EDUCATIONAL.—We are not called upon to do much work in this line, as most of 
the members are at school. _We have, however, been able to do a little to supple- 
ment it by illustrated lectures and practical talks. We are, however, looking 
forward to the new building and its advantages, when we shall be able to furnish a 
good supply of material for development. 


bo i 


38 


The Library has been well used, considering that no new books have been added. 
Out of a total membership of 262, there have been 239 readers with a circulation of 
2585 books, and as we have only 760 books on our shelves, and many of them never 
taken out, it shows how this branch is appreciated. We should like, therefore, in 
the face of these facts, to make an urgent appeal for more books. ; 

ATHLETIC.—Although the average attendance at the gymnasium classes has not 
been increased, yet the work has been good and the interest maintained. The 
regular clubs have been organized, and outings, paper chases and drives have been 
held as usual, and have been all carried to a successful issue. 

We are able to report the holding of our first Summer Camp, which was in every 
way a deeided success, and will become an established item in our prospectus. This 
Camp was composed of 23 workers and boys. 

SocraL.—The socials and entertainments given were eleven in all, and proved, as 
they usually do, to be of great interest and attraction. An interesting departure was 
the receptions to the various schools of the city during the winter. They proved a 
helpful means of increasing our membership, pleasing the boys, bringing the Associa- 
tion prominently before the parents, and at the same time developing many of our 
workers. 

At the close of this year we are losing our faithful and earnest Secretary, Mr. F, 
H. Cushing ; but as we have had to face a similar difficulty in the past, and God 
has always supplied our need, we do not fear, but look up to Him in faith. In 
Mr. Cushing’s removal we are losing one who has grown up among the boys, and 
has been a great blessing and help to many of them during his presence among them, 
both as one of their members and as the Secretary of the Department. He has been 


~ true to the trust God has given him, and we pray that having been so, God will use, 


train and fit him in his college course that he may become a man of power among 
young men and boys. 

In closing our report we would say that God has richly blessed us, and yet we have 
done so little compared to what we might have done. We have another year before 
us now full of opportunities, it remains for each one of us to go in and do our very 
best, knowing how short the time is, how many boys are budding into manhood 
without a knowledge of Christ, and how many are anxious about this and how 
pleasing this work is to God if we do it faithfully.
